5.1. Problem Overview, Serverless Architecture & FinOps Estimation 1. Problem Statement Modern learners and researchers manage thousands of unstructured multimodal assets (whiteboard photos, lecture slides, audio recordings, video demos).
Default filenames (IMG_091522.jpg, voice_record_01.m4a) convey zero semantic context. Manually searching for specific moments like “teacher reviewing matrix exercises” or “integration formula on board” requires tedious manual review. 2. Workshop Objectives Build and deploy EduMedia AI following an Event-Driven Serverless architecture on AWS:
Upload files directly to Amazon S3 (Private Bucket, SSE-S3 encryption). Buffer upload events via Amazon SQS with an automated Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ). Orchestrate AWS Lambda processing: Images: Amazon Rekognition extracts object labels and Vietnamese OCR. Audio/Video: Amazon Transcribe generates Vietnamese speech-to-text (vi-VN). Generate 256-dimensional semantic embeddings using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and persist catalog in Amazon DynamoDB. Natural language Vietnamese query routing powered by Amazon Bedrock (Nova Lite). End-to-end monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch Logs & Alarms. 3. System Architecture Diagram 3.1. Service Selection Rationale: The architecture strictly adheres to AWS Well-Architected Framework principles, choosing Serverless and Managed Services over traditional provisioning based on clear technical justifications:
Selected AWS Service Evaluated Alternative Cost Optimization Criteria High Availability (HA) Serverless / Managed Model Amazon S3 (Standard Storage) Amazon EFS / Amazon EBS $0.023 / GB / month. 13x cheaper than EFS ($0.30/GB). Direct Presigned URLs offload client upload/download traffic entirely, saving 100% of compute and bandwidth costs on backend APIs. Data durability of 99.999999999% (11 9s) alongside 99.99% designed Availability (99.9% SLA commitment), automatically replicated across at least 3 Availability Zones (AZs) in the Region. Managed Object Storage, eliminating disk volume provisioning, filesystem sizing, and storage server management. Amazon CloudFront (Web SPA CDN) EC2 Reverse Proxy (Nginx) / Public S3 Bucket Includes 1 TB Data Transfer Out & 10M HTTP/HTTPS requests/month Always Free for delivering the React Web SPA (agentsys-web-*), yielding $0.00 idle cost. Global edge points of presence with automatic TLS termination and burst absorption without self-managed proxy fleets. Managed Edge CDN, cleanly separating static Web UI distribution from private media and API endpoints. AWS Lambda (Python 3.12 Runtime) Amazon ECS (Fargate / EC2) $0.00 idle cost (Zero Idle Cost). Metered strictly per millisecond and GB-second during actual event execution. 1M free requests/month under AWS Free Tier. ECS Fargate incurs continuous base charges (~$15 - $30/month/task) even with zero traffic. Default Multi-AZ redundancy across the Region; scales instantaneously from 0 to thousands of concurrent executions without managing Auto Scaling Groups. Pure Serverless FaaS, eliminating OS patching, security kernel upgrades, and container runtime daemon maintenance. Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Application Load Balancer (ALB) / REST API Low cost of $1.00 / million requests (>70% cheaper than REST API at $3.50/M). Zero idle hourly charges compared to ALB (~$16 - $20/month base LCU cost). Native Multi-AZ fault tolerance; protected against L3/L4 DDoS attacks via default AWS Shield Standard and API Gateway account-level limits paired with application-layer rate limiting. Serverless HTTP API, native CORS handling, direct zero-overhead Lambda proxy routing. API authentication (verify_api_key enforcing X-API-Key / JWT) and rate limiting (slowapi 60 reqs/min/IP) are enforced at the FastAPI application tier. Amazon DynamoDB (On-Demand Mode) Amazon RDS Aurora (PostgreSQL / MySQL) $0.00 idle cost. Metered strictly per actual read/write request units (RRU/WRU) plus 25 GB Always Free storage. Aurora Serverless v2 requires a continuous minimum ACU allocation (~$35 - $60/month). Automatic synchronous data replication across 3 AZs; backed by a 99.99% SLA with single-digit millisecond query latency (<10ms). NoSQL Serverless Database, immune to connection pool exhaustion during Lambda scale bursts; zero schema migration downtime. Amazon SQS & DLQ (Message Queue) Amazon Kinesis Data Streams / Apache Kafka (MSK) $0.40 / million requests. 1 million requests free every month (Always Free). In contrast, Kinesis charges per Shard-hour ($11/month/shard) and MSK requires continuous cluster broker fees ($100+/month). Highly resilient distributed message queue across Multi-AZ (agentsys-ingest-queue 24-hour retention, 3 DLQs 14-day retention), buffering burst loads (MaximumConcurrency = 5) without downstream AI throttling. Fully Managed Queue, automatically batch-triggering Lambda Ingest workers and isolating corrupted payloads into Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ). Amazon Bedrock (Nova Pro / Nova Lite & Titan Embeddings V2) Self-hosted LLM on Amazon EC2 GPU (G4dn / G5) $0.06 / million input tokens (Nova Lite), $0.02 / million input tokens (Titan Embeddings V2), plus Cross-Region Inference (us.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0) costing mere pennies in testing. Self-hosting open-source LLMs on EC2 GPU (g4dn.xlarge or g5.xlarge) costs $380 – $750 USD/month continuously. Foundation models hosted on AWS high-performance GPU clusters with built-in high availability and automated inference load distribution. Serverless GenAI API (FaaS), requiring zero management of GPU hardware, CUDA drivers, vLLM containers, or inference scaling clusters. Amazon Rekognition & Transcribe Custom self-trained ML models on EC2 Amazon Transcribe billed at official rate $0.024 / minute ($0.0004 / second). Rekognition billed at $0.001 / API call (DetectLabels + DetectText = $0.002 / image). Eliminates R&D, data labeling, model training, and continuous hosting overhead. Purpose-built AWS AI services backed by 99.9% SLAs and automatic elastic concurrency. Pre-trained Managed AI Services: Transcribe natively optimized for Vietnamese speech-to-text (vi-VN); Rekognition handles object labeling (DetectLabels) and slide text/title extraction (DetectText) out-of-the-box without custom ML training. 4. FinOps Cost Modeling & Production Workload Estimates (AWS Region: us-east-1) Within the FCAJ project framework, operational expenditures are engineered following FinOps (Cloud Financial Management) principles based on two realistic deployment scenarios modeled via the AWS Pricing Calculator:
Official AWS Public Estimate: Official EduMedia AI Public Estimate (us-east-1 N. Virginia) 4.1. Scenario 1: Self-hosted Workshop & POC Evaluation (1 Tester) Evaluation Workload: 50 slide images, 5 audio files (20 total minutes), 100 Bedrock AI queries, 1 GB S3 storage, 2,000 Lambda & DynamoDB invocations. Gross Incurred Cost (Without Free Tier): $0.76 – $0.88 USD (~19,400 – 22,400 VND for completing the entire lab at Transcribe’s $0.024/min rate card). Net Invoiced Cost (With Free Tier): Pay only for Bedrock On-Demand (~$0.18 USD / ~4,500 VND), or $0.00 USD if using an account eligible for AWS Free Tier Credits. 4.2. Scenario 2: Department Class / Study Club Workload (100 – 200 Students / Month) Monthly workload: 1,500 lecture slides, 250 audio minutes, 2,000 Bedrock queries, 20 GB S3 storage + PUT/GET requests, 15,000 Lambda invocations, 50,000 SQS messages, 15,000 HTTP API Gateway requests, DynamoDB On-Demand (15k W / 60k R), 10 GB CloudFront DTO, 2 custom metrics + 0.5 GB logs + 7 CloudWatch Alarms.
AWS Service Production Workload (100 - 200 Students) Gross Cost (Without Free Tier) Standard Production Bill (With Always Free) Amazon Rekognition 1,500 images × 2 APIs = 3,000 calls $3.00 USD $3.00 USD (Year 1: $2.00) Amazon Transcribe 250 lecture minutes vi-VN $6.00 USD (Rate Card $0.024/min) $6.00 USD (Calculator: $1.50) Amazon Bedrock 2,000 queries Nova Pro (2.0M in + 0.6M out) + Titan Embed V2 (2.0M) $3.56 USD (Nova Pro $3.52 + Embed $0.04) $3.56 USD Amazon S3 20 GB Standard + PUT (2,000) / GET (10,000) requests $0.47 USD (Storage $0.46 + Reqs $0.01) $0.47 USD (Year 1: $0.35) AWS Lambda & SQS 15,000 invocations (512MB, 1.5s) + 50,000 SQS msgs $0.21 USD (Lambda $0.19 + SQS $0.02) $0.00 USD (Always Free: 1M Lambda + 1M SQS) Amazon API Gateway HTTP API v2 (15,000 requests/mo) $0.02 USD $0.02 USD Amazon DynamoDB On-Demand (15,000 writes + 60,000 reads, 0.02 GB) $0.02 USD $0.02 USD (< 25 GB Always Free) Amazon CloudFront 10 GB Data Transfer Out + 15,000 HTTPS reqs $0.85 USD $0.00 USD (Always Free 1 TB / 10M reqs) Amazon CloudWatch 2 custom metrics ($0.60) + 0.5 GB logs ($0.25) + 7 alarms ($0.70) $1.55 USD $0.00 USD (Always Free: 10 metrics / 10 alarms / 5 GB) TOTAL Full System for 100 - 200 Students $15.68 USD / month (Calculator Transcribe: $11.18) $13.07 USD / month (Calculator Direct: $10.14; Net: $8.57) CURRENCY CONVERSION Exchange Rate: 1 USD = 25,500 VND ~400,000 VND / month (Calculator Transcribe: ~285,000 VND) ~333,000 VND / month (Calculator Direct: ~259,000 VND; Net: ~219,000 VND) PER-STUDENT COST Scale of 100 – 200 Students 1,999 – 3,998 VND / student / month 1,666 – 3,333 VND / student / month AWS Pricing Calculator vs Rate Card Reconciliation:
On the official AWS Pricing Calculator (us-east-1 N. Virginia), all 11 resource entries across 10 AWS services total 10.14 USD / month (121.68 USD / 12 months): Rekognition $3.00, Transcribe $1.50, Bedrock Nova Pro $3.52, Bedrock Titan Embeddings V2 $0.04, S3 $0.47, DynamoDB $0.02, SQS $0.02 (pre-Free Tier), API Gateway $0.02, Lambda $0.00, CloudFront $0.00, and CloudWatch $1.55 (pre-Free Tier). Excluding AI APIs, the entire Serverless compute, queue, database, CDN, and monitoring tier totals only $0.51 USD / month after Always Free allowances, scaling automatically to $0.00 USD when idle. Architecture Diagram vs Cost Model Reconciliation: The architecture diagram captures the complete end-to-end production topology—spanning Frontend Edge delivery via Amazon CloudFront CDN backed by Amazon S3 Static SPA Hosting (agentsys-web-*, validated at d27yx88v3wm0yt.cloudfront.net in section 5.5) alongside the Backend Serverless ingestion and AI processing pipeline in us-east-1—aligning 100% with every line item modeled in the AWS Pricing Calculator estimate. 5. title: Blog 1 - Serverless Media Processing: Why I Avoid Direct S3 Lambda Triggers
content:
Author: Do Tran Minh Phuc (Student ID: 23120156 — VNUHCM University of Science) Program: First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) 2026 — AWS Vietnam Associated Project: EduMedia AI — Multi-modal Media Retrieval System on Serverless AWS Publication Channel: AWS Study Group Community (Facebook Post) Serverless Media Processing in EduMedia AI: Why I Avoid Direct S3 Lambda Triggers When designing media ingestion for EduMedia AI, my initial instinct was: whenever an object lands on S3, directly invoke the Lambda ingest worker. Files trigger code instantaneously without an extra queue, matching conventional serverless tutorials.
However, during high-volume load testing simulating peak classroom submissions (50–100 slide decks and audio recordings uploaded simultaneously), this push-based direct trigger architecture exposed three critical pitfalls:
1. Three Critical Pitfalls of Push-Based S3 Direct Triggers Lambda Internal Queue is a Black Box:
S3 invokes Lambda asynchronously. Events land inside an AWS-managed internal queue that lacks real-time queue depth metrics. Engineers cannot monitor pending message count, pause ingestion, or purge obsolete events during emergencies.
Concurrency Exhaustion & “Noisy Neighbor” Impact:
Under rapid bursts, Lambda scales containers aggressively. This not only consumes regional account concurrency (throttling critical search APIs), but also overwhelms downstream services like Amazon DynamoDB write thresholds and Amazon Transcribe concurrent job limits. Applying Reserved Concurrency simply causes events to back up and age out in the internal queue.
Silent Event Loss (Silent Failure):
Lambda async invocations default to 2 retries (3 total attempts). If attempts exhaust or exceed the internal retention window (default 6 hours) without an On-Failure Destination, the event drops silently. Even if CloudWatch logs AsyncEventsDropped, event metadata evaporates forever while raw S3 objects remain stranded and unprocessed.
2. Architecture Comparison: Push-Based vs. Decoupled SQS + DLQ Figure: Comparison between the Push-based Anti-pattern and the Pull-based SQS + DLQ Claim Check Best Practice implemented in EduMedia AI.
3. Solution: Pull-Based Flow via SQS + DLQ S3 (ObjectCreated) ──> SQS Ingest Queue ──> Lambda Ingest ──> DynamoDB & S3 Output This architecture addresses each failure mode through four architectural pillars:
3.1. Load Regulation with MaximumConcurrency Batching (BatchSize = 5) alone does not prevent over-scaling because AWS Event Source Mapping (ESM) pollers scale aggressively when queues build up.
By configuring ScalingConfig: MaximumConcurrency = 5 on the ESM, the system enforces a strict ceiling of ~25 in-flight items at any moment (5 workers × batch 5), safeguarding downstream throughput regardless of burst size.
3.2. Partial Failure Handling (ReportBatchItemFailures) By default, if 1 out of 5 batch items fails, SQS retries the entire batch. Enabling ReportBatchItemFailures and returning failed item IDs ensures that ESM deletes the 4 successful items and retains only the failed item for targeted redelivery.
3.3. DLQ Safety Net via Claim Check Pattern Configuring maxReceiveCount = 3 on SQS routes repeatedly failing messages into the Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ):
Claim Check: Messages carry lightweight pointer metadata (~1 KB) while raw media files reside safely in S3 (uploads/). Self-Healing Redrive: The DLQ retains messages for 14 days with CloudWatch alarms notifying SNS. Once a bug fix deploys, clicking “Start redrive” transfers messages back to the primary queue for automated re-processing without user intervention. 3.4. Idempotency & Recursive Loop Defense Idempotency: SQS Standard guarantees at-least-once delivery. The Lambda worker uses object_key as Partition Key with DynamoDB conditional expressions (attribute_not_exists) to prevent duplicate Transcribe jobs and race conditions. Loop Prevention: S3 event notifications listen strictly on the uploads/ prefix, while generated thumbnails and transcripts write to thumbs/ and transcripts/, eliminating self-triggering loops. 4. Summary Takeaway In serverless architectures, engineering rigor is not about wiring managed services together; it is about controlling state transitions under load bursts and designing self-healing failure recovery into the data path.

title: Event 1
content:
Event 1: AWS First Cloud AI Journey - Community Day Date: Saturday, August 22, 2026 (09:00 AM - 12:00 PM) Location: AWS Vietnam Office, 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Ben Nghe Ward, District 1, Ho Chi Minh City Role: Intern attendee Organized by: AWS First Cloud Journey (FCJ) & AWS Community Personal Check-in Photo: See Section 6. Event Check-in & Souvenir Photos (note regarding wearing a mask at the first event) 1. Event Overview AWS First Cloud AI Journey - Community Day (August 2026) was an in-depth technical knowledge-sharing conference organized by the First Cloud Journey (FCJ) community at the AWS Vietnam Office (26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower).
The event featured 7 intensive sharing sessions spanning across: Serverless Architecture, Database Optimization & Archiving Strategy, AI/DevOps, Cloud Native, and Generative AI, bringing together 9 seasoned engineers and technology leaders from leading enterprises.
Featured Speakers: Lâm Tuấn Kiệt (Kiet Lam) — Senior DevOps Engineer, FPT Software Lý Hoàng Việt (Viet Ly) — DevOps Engineer, VPBank (AWS Community Builder) Nguyễn Tuấn Kiệt (Kiet Nguyen) — Software Engineer / Data Engineer, VPBank Huỳnh Hoàng Long (Long Huynh) — Solution Architect, eCloudvalley Ngọc Trần (Ngoc Tran) — Service Reliability Engineer Intern, Accenture Bảo Huỳnh (Bao Huynh) — Cloud Native Developer, Endava Viet Nam Xuân Lê (Xuan Le) — Data Analytics & Insights Nghị Danh (Nghi Danh) — AI Engineer, Renova Cloud Vĩ Trần (Vi Tran) — CloudOps Engineer, VIB 2. Session 1: DevOps AI Development Application with AWS Serverless Speaker: Lam Tuan Kiet (Kiet Lam) — Senior DevOps Engineer at FPT Software 2.1. Essence of Serverless Computing Mr. Kiet opened the session by explaining the core philosophy of Serverless — offloading underlying infrastructure management completely to AWS:
Focus on Code: Development teams focus 100% on feature delivery and business logic without managing server provisioning, Load Balancer configuration, or operating system patching. Automatic Scaling & Scale-to-Zero: Infrastructure dynamically scales with real-time incoming traffic and automatically scales down to zero when idle. Cost-effective (Pay-as-you-go): Billed strictly based on exact invocation count and precise execution runtime (in milliseconds). Zero idle cost incurred. 2.2. Event-driven Architecture & Core Serverless Services The architecture follows the Event Trigger ➔ AWS Lambda Execution ➔ Response execution flow:
AWS Service Technical Role AWS Lambda Multi-language serverless compute engine executed on-demand, deeply integrated with AWS services Amazon API Gateway Managed traffic ingestion gateway providing routing, throttling, and direct integrations with Lambda/SQS Amazon DynamoDB Fully managed, single-digit millisecond latency NoSQL database with auto-scaling throughput Amazon S3 Durable object storage for media assets, unstructured data, and static Single Page Application (SPA) hosting 2.3. Traditional vs. Serverless Application Comparison Criteria Traditional Application (VM / Monolith / Container) Serverless Application (Lambda / API Gateway) Infrastructure Self-managed Server, OS, Auto Scaling Groups, manual patching 100% managed by AWS Deployment Unit Monolith service, Docker container image, Virtual Machine Function (Lambda), API Route, Event Handler Scaling Complex configuration (Nginx, ALB, Kubernetes HPA…), minute-scale scaling Instant, automated scaling per request invocation Cost Model Billed 24/7 continuously regardless of actual workload Only billed during active execution + data transfer High Availability (HA) Requires explicit Multi-AZ configuration & Failover design Built-in Multi-AZ High Availability at the service layer 2.4. 6 Real-World Trade-offs and Engineering Solutions Mr. Kiet highlighted that Serverless is not a silver bullet and discussed 6 practical production trade-offs:
Cold Start Latency: New Lambda instances require ~2-3 seconds to initialize the execution container and libraries.
➜ Solution: Enable Provisioned Concurrency (keeping 2-3 warm instances ready) for latency-critical endpoints. Local Debugging & Tracing Complexity: Difficult to replicate distributed cloud triggers and IAM permissions locally.
➜ Solution: Establish dedicated cloud Development environments on AWS, automated via CI/CD pipelines for direct testing. Vendor Lock-in: Code and trigger bindings are tied to AWS-native APIs and managed services. Cost Predictability under Continuous High Traffic: For applications with sustained high concurrency 24/7, Serverless can exceed container hosting costs.
➜ Rule: Start with Serverless for unpredictable or variable workloads; consider migrating to container-based architectures (ECS/EKS) once steady baseline traffic is established. Package Size Limit (250 MB): Heavy AI/ML dependencies can exceed unzipped package limits.
➜ Solution: Modularize shared dependencies into Lambda Layers. Database Connection Exhaustion: Hundreds of concurrently spawned Lambda instances can overwhelm relational databases (PostgreSQL/MySQL).
➜ Solution: Deploy Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the database to handle centralized Connection Pooling. 2.5. 4 Serverless Application Patterns Pattern 1 - Synchronous API: Client ➔ API Gateway ➔ Lambda Handler ➔ DynamoDB / RDS. Pattern 2 - Authentication & Authorization: Client ➔ Amazon Cognito User Pool / API Gateway Custom Authorizer ➔ Lambda. Pattern 3 - Scheduled CronJobs: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler periodically triggering Lambda (e.g. nightly data aggregation). Pattern 4 - Asynchronous Event Processing: Producer ➔ Amazon SQS Queue ➔ Lambda (e.g. batch email notifications, asynchronous video processing). 2.6. Monorepo Project Structure for Serverless Applications Mr. Kiet shared the production project layout used at FPT Software:
apps/: Each subfolder represents an isolated Lambda function handler. packages/shared-library/: Shared utility code (standard error responses, TypeScript types, loggers). packages/infra/: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) defining Lambda configurations, API Gateway paths, and IAM roles. 2.7. Q&A Highlights Live Workshop Discussion Question (Trung Kien - Software Engineer):
Why evaluate Serverless for cost optimization instead of traditional architectures? Speaker (Lam Tuan Kiet):
Consider internal banking portals: Staff only use them during business hours (8 hours/day, Mon-Fri). Running traditional servers 24/7 wastes money during the remaining 16 hours and weekends. Serverless scales to zero during idle periods, saving 100% of off-hour compute costs. Only when traffic becomes steady around the clock should container migration be considered. 3. Session 2: Optimize Database Cost & Performance with Data Archiving Strategy Speakers: Ly Hoang Viet (Viet Ly) — AWS Community Builder, DevOps Engineer at VPBank Nguyen Tuan Kiet (Kiet Nguyen) — Software Engineer / Data Engineer at VPBank 3.1. Enterprise Challenge: Operational Database Growth Over years of continuous operation, banking databases grow to hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes:
Skyrocketing Storage Costs: Provisioning high-performance SSD storage on Amazon RDS or DynamoDB is expensive. Degraded Query Performance: Multi-million-row tables cause query latency degradation even with indexing. Impacting User Experience: Banking customers experience delays during financial operations. 3.2. Data Tiering Strategy: Hot Data vs. Cold Data Criteria Hot Data Cold Data (Historical) Characteristics Recent transactional records (< 1 year / < 90 days) Historical records (> 1 year / > 90 days) Access Frequency Queried continuously daily for live operations Rarely accessed (audit, historical inquiries) Optimal Storage Amazon RDS PostgreSQL / MySQL Amazon S3 Data Lake + Amazon Athena 3.3. Archiving Pipeline Architecture The VPBank engineering team presented an automated pipeline with two main flows:
Flow 1: Initial Full Load (Migrating Baseline Historical Data) AWS DMS (Database Migration Service): Extracts historical data beyond the cutoff (e.g. > 90 days) from RDS to Amazon S3 as Raw Parquet files. AWS Glue Job: Ingests Raw Parquet, performs Deep Partitioning (/year=YYYY/month=MM/day=DD/), and writes to the S3 Curated bucket. Purge Script: Safely removes archived records from the source RDS database. Flow 2: Daily Incremental Load Amazon EventBridge: Automatically triggers the ETL workflow during off-peak night hours to avoid production I/O contention. Step Functions + AWS Lambda + AWS Glue: Ingests the oldest day’s cold records, converts to Parquet, partitions, and stores in S3 Curated. Purge Task: Deletes corresponding rows from RDS to keep database footprint at an optimal steady state (e.g. capping at 50 GB instead of growing past 100 GB+). Amazon Athena: Acts as a Serverless SQL query engine allowing staff or reporting tools to query S3 cold data using standard ANSI SQL without reloading into databases. 3.4. Live Demo on RDS PostgreSQL Mr. Nguyen Tuan Kiet demonstrated the workflow live:
Configured a 90-day cutoff timestamp on PostgreSQL. Executed AWS DMS extraction of cold data to S3 Raw bucket. Ran AWS Glue job to partition data into S3 Curated (Year/Month/Day). Successfully executed the purge script, deleting 629 records from the source table. Queried archived data in Amazon Athena with rapid execution via Partition Pruning. 3.5. Cost Breakdown Analysis Initial Load (DMS C3 Medium, 50 GB Storage, Single-AZ + 2 Glue DPUs): 100 GB Data Volume: DMS runtime 4h ($0.48) + Glue runtime 1h ($1.00) ≈ $1.48 1 TB Data Volume: DMS runtime 24h ($2.88) + Glue runtime 6h ($6.00) ≈ $8.88 Daily Incremental Load (2 Glue workers per job): 5 minutes/day runtime: Archive Only = $2.20/month | Archive + Purge = $4.40/month 10 minutes/day runtime: Archive Only = $4.40/month | Archive + Purge = $8.80/month 20 minutes/day runtime: Archive Only = $8.80/month | Archive + Purge = $17.60/month Associated costs for Lambda, Step Functions, EventBridge, and DynamoDB control table are negligible (~$0/month). 3.6. 5 Key Takeaways Archive cold data: Proactively separate historical data from primary OLTP databases. Use incremental processing: Process daily batches to keep runtime and resource costs minimal. Optimize data format: Always leverage columnar Parquet with Deep Partitioning. Right-size compute: Match Glue DPU and DMS instance sizing to actual workload volume. Keep data accessible: Ensure cold data remains instantly queryable via Amazon Athena. 3.7. In-Depth Q&A Q1: Multi-AZ / Multi-Region Replication Question: How to ensure consistency and prevent downtime when migrating large datasets across regions? Answer: AWS DMS supports Multi-AZ deployment. Migrations filter historical records by timestamp cutoff, preventing write locks or conflicts with live transactions. Q2: Accelerating Cold Data Queries Question: How to maximize query speed on cold S3 data? Answer: Define fine-grained partition keys (Year/Month/Day/Client ID) for Athena partition pruning. For enterprise environments requiring ACID guarantees and time-travel queries, implement Open Table Formats like Apache Iceberg or Apache Hudi on S3 Data Lake. Q3: Amazon Redshift at VPBank Question: What is the primary use case for Amazon Redshift at VPBank? Answer: Redshift is utilized as an SQL Data Transformation Engine. The team loads data from Data Lake to Redshift and uses standard SQL for complex analytical transformations without having to manage Apache Spark clusters. 4. Session 3: Diffusion & OCR — Generative AI on AWS Serverless Infrastructure Speaker: Huynh Hoang Long (Long Huynh) — Solution Architect at eCloudvalley 4.1. Serverless Text-to-Image Generation Architecture Fully Serverless architectural workflow:
Frontend Hosting: Single Page Application (SPA) hosted on Amazon S3 and distributed globally via Amazon CloudFront CDN. API & Routing: Amazon API Gateway receives client requests and triggers AWS Lambda. Prompt Enrichment: Lambda invokes Claude Haiku 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock to expand short Vietnamese prompts into detailed, photorealistic descriptive English prompts. Image Synthesis: Lambda forwards the enriched prompt to Stability AI (Stable Image) on Bedrock to render high-resolution visuals. Storage & Delivery: Rendered images are stored in Amazon S3 and secure CDN URLs are returned to the client. 4.2. Live Demo: “DemoAI — Image ⇌ Text” Features demonstrated live:
Image to Text (OCR): Text extraction and scene understanding using Amazon Rekognition combined with Bedrock. Text to Image: Customization options including Cinematic styles, aspect ratios (16:9, 1:1), negative prompts (removing watermarks, low quality), and seed control. Pay-as-you-go cost model with zero idle baseline expense. 5. Key Learnings and Practical Value Attending the AWS First Cloud AI Journey - Community Day provided high-value engineering insights:
Modern Cloud-Native Architectural Thinking: Clear criteria for balancing Serverless agility and Containerized throughput in production environments. Enterprise Database Lifecycle Mastery: The Hot/Cold Data Archiving pattern (DMS + S3 + Glue + Athena) drastically reduces storage costs while retaining historical data accessibility. Applied GenAI Integration: Practical patterns for chaining foundational LLMs (Claude Haiku via Amazon Bedrock) for prompt engineering before routing into generative diffusion models. 6. Event Check-in & Souvenir Photos Figure: Personal check-in photo at 26th Floor Bitexco. (Note: As this was the very first event I attended, I inadvertently kept my mask on when taking the selfie; my full unmasked face can be cross-verified with the homepage portrait and clear-face check-in photos in Event 2 and Event 3).

title: Blog 2 - Optimizing DynamoDB Queries: Why I Ditched Scan + FilterExpression for GSI
content:
Author: Do Tran Minh Phuc (Student ID: 23120156 — VNUHCM-University of Science) Program: First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) 2026 — AWS Vietnam Related Project: EduMedia AI — Smart Lecture Storage & Retrieval Platform on AWS Published Community: AWS Study Group Community (Facebook) (Submitted — Pending Admin Approval) Optimizing DynamoDB Queries in EduMedia AI: Why I Ditched Scan + FilterExpression for GSI While building EduMedia AI (a serverless multimodal media catalog and semantic retrieval platform on AWS), one of the most fundamental requirements was filtering media records by category (category values like study, music, video, docs, raw…).
Coming from a relational SQL background to NoSQL with DynamoDB, I initially made a textbook mistake: using Scan with a FilterExpression, assuming it behaves like a WHERE clause in MySQL or PostgreSQL.
When the database holds only a few hundred items, the API feels snappy and everything seems fine. But looking under the hood at DynamoDB’s physical read and billing mechanics reveals that relying on Scan + FilterExpression for real-time queries is an awful solution for both cloud bill and tail latency.
1. FilterExpression Does Not Save RCU as Most People Expect In the DynamoDB SDK (boto3), passing FilterExpression into Scan makes it tempting to think the engine only reads and charges for items matching the condition. Under the hood, DynamoDB’s storage nodes actually execute in three distinct phases:
Disk Read: DynamoDB scans physical partitions sequentially, pulling raw data blocks from disk into memory up to a hard ceiling of 1 MB per page. RCU Billing: The system calculates and deducts Read Capacity Units (RCU) on 100% of the raw data read from disk, regardless of whether each item matches your filter or not (AWS pricing rule: each 4 KB block costs 1 RCU for Strongly Consistent Reads, or 0.5 RCU for Eventually Consistent Reads). RAM Filtering: Only after the full RCU fee has already been charged does DynamoDB apply your FilterExpression in memory to discard non-matching records before sending the payload back to the client. In short: FilterExpression only saves network bandwidth back to your client. The disk read complexity remains O(N) across the entire table. If your table holds 1 million items and only 20 match category = ‘study’, you still pay RCU for reading all 1 million items.
2. The “Empty Page” Trap (Empty Page Pagination) Freezing Lambda Beyond high RCU consumption, Scan with FilterExpression creates a nasty tail latency problem due to the 1 MB page boundary:
The 1 MB ceiling applies to raw data read from disk before filtering, not to the size of the final response array. Suppose our AgentSysMediaMetadata table grows to 400 MB. If the first 1 MB block read from disk contains no items with category = ‘study’, DynamoDB still returns an empty array (Items: []) along with a LastEvaluatedKey cursor. The search Lambda function is then forced into an iterative while loop, making repeated network round-trips to DynamoDB to scan consecutive 1 MB blocks until it collects 20 items for the UI. As a result, a simple catalog list API can see latency explode from 20ms to several seconds. This bloats Lambda execution duration (GB-seconds) and risks hitting API Gateway’s 29-second hard timeout on large datasets.
3. Architecture Comparison: Scan vs. GSI Targeted Query Here is the architectural comparison between the two approaches:
Figure 3.2: Physical storage mechanics contrasting the Anti-pattern (Scan + FilterExpression) against Best Practice (Query via GSI category-index).
4. The EduMedia AI Solution: Switching to Query on Global Secondary Index (GSI) To eliminate full table scans without modifying the primary key file_id on the base table AgentSysMediaMetadata, I configured a Global Secondary Index (GSI) named category-index:
Partition Key: category - Groups all records sharing the same category into a single logical partition. Sort Key: created_at - Pre-sorts records chronologically on disk (ISO-8601 UTC). When fetching latest media, code doesn’t need application-tier sorting. Projection: INCLUDE - Base items in EduMedia AI carry heavy payloads (such as long lecture transcripts used for AI search). Setting Projection: ALL would duplicate all heavy attributes to the GSI, doubling storage and WCU footprint. We only INCLUDE the lightweight fields needed for UI grid rendering: filename, thumbnail_url, status, duration (the base table’s partition key file_id is automatically projected to the GSI by DynamoDB). With the GSI created, Lambda code switches from Scan to a direct Query:
import os import boto3 from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key TABLE_NAME = os.environ.get('MEDIA_METADATA_TABLE', 'AgentSysMediaMetadata') dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb', region_name='ap-southeast-1') table = dynamodb.Table(TABLE_NAME) def get_media_by_category(category_name: str, limit: int = 20, cursor: dict = None): # Direct Query against GSI partition instead of full-table scan params = { 'IndexName': 'category-index', 'KeyConditionExpression': Key('category').eq(category_name), 'ScanIndexForward': False, # Fetch newest items first based on created_at 'Limit': limit } if cursor: params['ExclusiveStartKey'] = cursor response = table.query(**params) return { 'items': response.get('Items', []), 'next_cursor': response.get('LastEvaluatedKey') } Under-the-Hood Difference with GSI Query: Direct Partition Routing: DynamoDB hashes the category = ‘study’ value to immediately jump to the exact storage partition holding study data, skipping all other categories entirely (0 RCU). Reading Only What Is Needed (Limit=20): Because there is no FilterExpression, Limit=20 tells DynamoDB to stop reading disk right after retrieving the first 20 records chronologically. Single Network Round-Trip: No more empty pages or Lambda while loops. API response latency stays consistently around 10ms. 5. Practical Benchmark: Scan vs. GSI Query Looking at concrete production metrics from EduMedia AI, assume AgentSysMediaMetadata holds 100,000 items averaging 4 KB per item (total table size: 400 MB). When a user browses the 20 newest items in category study (using Eventually Consistent Read, where each 4 KB consumes 0.5 RCU):
Evaluation Criteria Scan + FilterExpression Query on GSI (category-index) Disk Retrieval Method Sequential full table scan Direct partition routing via Hash Key Data Read from Disk 400 MB (reads all 100,000 items) At most 80 KB (only first 20 items) Network Calls from Lambda At least 400 requests (1 MB/page limit) 1 request RCU Cost per API Call 50,000 RCU (100,000 × 0.5 RCU) ≤ 10 RCU (even lower with INCLUDE) Response Latency Several seconds to Timeout (grows with table size) ~5 ms – 15 ms (constant regardless of table size) Switching to a GSI query slashed 99.98% of RCU consumption per category query while locking latency to predictable milliseconds.
6. Architectural Trade-offs with GSI In cloud architecture, there is no free lunch. Implementing GSI requires weighing three trade-offs:
Write Amplification: Whenever the Ingest Worker Lambda inserts a new file or updates metadata on the base table, DynamoDB triggers an asynchronous background write to the GSI partition, consuming additional WCU. Limiting attributes via Projection: INCLUDE significantly reduces this overhead. Eventual Consistency: When Ingest Worker writes data into the base table, DynamoDB replicates attributes to the GSI asynchronously. GSIs only support Eventually Consistent Reads. This replication lag is typically within 10–50ms, which easily satisfies media browsing requirements. Hot Partition Risk: A single physical DynamoDB partition maxes out at 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU. For AgentSys, category handles normal traffic comfortably. For ultra-high traffic apps with tens of thousands of requests per second hitting one category, Write Sharding (appending random suffixes like study#1, study#2…) is needed to distribute load across physical partitions. 7. Key Takeaways The biggest practical lesson from building AgentSys with DynamoDB:
Never bring relational SELECT * … WHERE thinking into Scan + FilterExpression for end-user APIs. FilterExpression filters data only after you have been charged full RCU. In NoSQL, always determine your Access Patterns upfront to design the right Partition Key, Sort Key, and GSI from day one. Publication Evidence (Pending Admin Approval):

5.2. Environment Setup, AWS CLI, SAM, IAM Least-Privilege & Enabling Amazon Bedrock Model Access 1. Prerequisites & Tooling Setup Before getting started, ensure the following developer tools are configured locally:
AWS Account with AdministratorAccess or permissions to provision IAM Roles, S3, DynamoDB, Lambda, SQS, API Gateway, and CloudWatch. AWS CLI v2: Configured via aws configure. AWS SAM CLI: Tooling for building and deploying Serverless applications. Python 3.12 & Node.js 20+ (for running the Web UI). Verify AWS CLI Configuration: aws sts get-caller-identity aws configure get region Ensure the returned region is us-east-1 (N. Virginia).
2. Setting up Cost Guardrails (AWS Budgets) To guarantee zero unexpected charges during development:
Open the AWS Management Console → Search for AWS Budgets. Select Create budget → Cost budget. Name: My Zero-Spend Budget → Monthly budget limit: $1.00 USD (Zero-Spend protection). Configure an email notification trigger when actual spend exceeds threshold to ensure $0.00 USD billing. 3. Amazon Bedrock Model Access Management (Automated On-Demand Enablement) Under the latest AWS Bedrock operational policies, access management for foundation models has been streamlined into fully serverless automated enablement:
Model Access Retirement Notice & Instant Availability: For Amazon Serverless Foundation Models (including Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and Amazon Nova Lite / Nova Pro), AWS has officially retired manual model access application workflows. Models are now automatically enabled on-demand across all AWS commercial regions upon first invocation (InvokeModel or Converse API). Developers no longer need to submit manual use-case forms or await approval badges. IAM Least-Privilege Governance: Model invocation boundaries are now strictly governed by standard IAM Policies attached to Lambda execution roles (bedrock:InvokeModel) and Service Control Policies (SCPs), ensuring zero-trust governance directly via Infrastructure as Code (SAM). Note: For select third-party partner models (such as Anthropic Claude via AWS Marketplace), accounts may prompt for a one-time use-case registration prior to first invocation.
4. IAM Least-Privilege Architecture The SAM template (infra/template.yaml) defines three strictly segregated execution roles following least-privilege principles, mapped 1:1 to each Lambda function’s operational scope:
IngestFunctionRole (agentsys-ingest - lines 260-315 in template.yaml): S3 Access (ReadMediaObjects): s3:GetObject on uploads/* to retrieve raw media; s3:PutObject on thumbs/* and transcripts/* to store generated thumbnails and full Transcribe outputs. AI / ML Ingestion: Slide label and text/formula extraction (rekognition:DetectLabels, rekognition:DetectText); speech transcription pipeline control (transcribe:StartTranscriptionJob, transcribe:GetTranscriptionJob). DynamoDB Access (DynamoWrite): Status persistence and chunk writes (dynamodb:PutItem, dynamodb:GetItem, dynamodb:UpdateItem, dynamodb:Scan, dynamodb:Query, dynamodb:BatchWriteItem, dynamodb:DescribeTable) on table AgentSysMediaMetadata and GSI category-index. Amazon Bedrock (BedrockInvoke): Foundation model invocation (bedrock:InvokeModel) for amazon.nova-lite-v1:0, amazon.nova-pro-v1:0, and amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0. CloudWatch Custom Metrics (CustomMetrics): Operational telemetry publishing (cloudwatch:PutMetricData) strictly conditioned on cloudwatch:namespace: AgentSys. SQS Ingestion Event: SQS consumer permissions on agentsys-ingest-queue. AggregatorFunctionRole (agentsys-aggregator - lines 355-402 in template.yaml): DynamoDB Streams & Table (DynamoDBStreamAndTableAccess): Stream event processing (dynamodb:DescribeStream, dynamodb:GetRecords, dynamodb:GetShardIterator, dynamodb:ListStreams); keyed chunk reading and updates (dynamodb:GetItem, dynamodb:BatchGetItem, dynamodb:UpdateItem, dynamodb:Query, dynamodb:Scan, dynamodb:DescribeTable) on table AgentSysMediaMetadata. Amazon Bedrock (BedrockInvocation): Summary synthesis invocation (bedrock:InvokeModel) on amazon.nova-lite-v1:0 and amazon.nova-pro-v1:0. SQS Stream DLQ (SQSStreamDLQAccess): Forwarding unrecoverable stream events (sqs:SendMessage) to AggregatorStreamDLQ. CloudWatch Custom Metrics (CustomMetrics): Emitting operational metrics (cloudwatch:PutMetricData) to namespace AgentSys. ApiFunctionRole (agentsys-api - lines 435-502 in template.yaml): S3 Presigned Access (PresignUploads): Generating Presigned PUT URLs for direct uploads (uploads/*, direct/*), Presigned GET URLs for secure media/thumbnail delivery (thumbs/*, uploads/*), and s3:DeleteObject for asset cleanup. DynamoDB Access (DynamoAccess): Media metadata CRUD and catalog querying (dynamodb:GetItem, dynamodb:PutItem, dynamodb:DeleteItem, dynamodb:Scan, dynamodb:Query, dynamodb:BatchWriteItem) across AgentSysMediaMetadata and GSI category-index. Amazon Bedrock (BedrockInvoke): Foundation model inference permissions (bedrock:InvokeModel, bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream) for amazon.nova-lite-v1:0, amazon.nova-pro-v1:0, and amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0 powering AI Search Planner and Converse API endpoints. SQS Ingestion Dispatch (IngestQueueSend): Queue dispatching permissions (sqs:SendMessage) on agentsys-ingest-queue when clients invoke media processing or reprocessing routes (/process, /reprocess). CloudWatch Custom Metrics (CustomMetrics): Publishing operational telemetry (cloudwatch:PutMetricData) to namespace AgentSys. Health Check & Diagnostics (HealthPings, HealthBucket, HealthTable): Subsystem diagnostics for the /health endpoint (sts:GetCallerIdentity, rekognition:ListCollections, transcribe:ListTranscriptionJobs, bedrock:GetFoundationModel, bedrock:GetInferenceProfile, s3:ListBucket on MediaBucket, dynamodb:DescribeTable on MetadataTable). 5. Running Automated Unit Tests Run the local unit test suite with Pytest to verify core modules (ingestion pipeline, API authentication, and Bedrock query handling) before deploying to AWS:
# 1. Clone the EduMedia AI repository git clone https://github.com/Mphuc310771/edumedia-ai.git cd edumedia-ai # 2. Create and activate Python virtual environment python -m venv venv # Windows: .\venv\Scripts\activate # Linux/macOS: source venv/bin/activate # 3. Install dependencies and run 143 unit test cases pip install -r requirements.txt pytest -v Expected: Test suite passes, confirming business logic and IAM access assumptions function as designed.
6. Building and Deploying with AWS SAM From the edumedia-ai project directory:
sam build -t infra/template.yaml sam deploy --guided Guided Deployment Parameters: Parameter Recommended Value Purpose Stack Name edumedia-ai CloudFormation Stack Name (or agentsys) AWS Region us-east-1 Target AWS Region Parameter ApiKey dev-local-api-key API Protection Key (X-API-Key header) Parameter FrontendOriginUrl * (or your Vercel/CloudFront domain) Allowed Origin for CORS Confirm changes before deploy Y Review CloudFormation changeset Allow SAM CLI IAM role creation Y Grant SAM permission to create IAM roles After deployment succeeds, record the values in Outputs:

Session 1: Community Spirit, AI-Era Hiring Realities & FCJ Build-a-thon Core Values Speaker: Mr. Nguyen Gia Hung — Head of Solutions Architecture at AWS Vietnam & Cambodia; Founder First Cloud Journey (FCJ/FCAJ) & AWS Study Group. About the Speaker: Mr. Nguyen Gia Hung is the Head of Solutions Architecture for AWS across Vietnam and Cambodia, with over 17 years of enterprise cloud architecture leadership. He is the founder and guiding spirit of the First Cloud Journey (FCAJ) initiative and the AWS Study Group community, directly securing sponsorship from global/ASEAN AWS executives and enterprise partners to build high-impact cloud internship and career pathways for university students.
2.1. Cloud Stature, AWS Ecosystem & Long-Term Investment in Vietnam Mr. Hung reflected on AWS’s strategic journey in Vietnam since 2015:
Unlike typical short-term software subscription models, AWS focuses on deep, sustainable investments in people, local talent, and foundational infrastructure: establishing official entities in HCMC (2017) and Hanoi (2019), launching Edge Locations, Local Zones, and progressing toward future AWS Region development in Vietnam. AWS serves as the principal profit engine of Amazon, powering major commercial banks, fintechs, and tech enterprises in Vietnam (VPBank, Techcombank, VIB, VNG, MoMo, Masan, Grab…). AWS Investment History in Vietnam (2015 – 2026) Diverse Customer Base in Vietnam 2.2. “AWS is your competitive edge, not a job title” Mr. Hung emphasized that Cloud and AWS are no longer isolated job titles, but mandatory baseline competencies for all software engineers:
Regardless of role — whether AI Engineer, Backend Developer, Data Engineer, or DevOps — proficiency in Cloud infrastructure serves as a vital competitive edge. In the generative AI era, hiring managers expect candidates to possess both solid Computer Science fundamentals and the ability to leverage modern AI tools effectively. 2.3. Core Mental Models for Young Engineers Drawing from over 20 years of technical leadership, Mr. Hung shared essential mental models:
The Power of Brotherhood: “Sharks swim in schools; only goldfish drift aimlessly.” Industry challenges are increasingly complex; engineers must cultivate reliable, collaborative networks to sustain long-term career growth. Jevons Paradox in Software Engineering: As AI reduces software development costs, the total volume of software will explode exponentially. More software inherently demands greater human accountability (human-in-the-loop) and advanced troubleshooting capabilities under production pressure. Two Fundamental Engineering Inquiries: Every technical assessment boils down to two core proofs: Have you personally built and deployed a production-grade system? When critical incidents arise, can you debug and resolve them down to root causes? “Pay it forward” Culture: Prioritize contributing to the community and team before seeking personal perks or voicing complaints. Resilience & Self-Investment: “If you hesitate to invest in your own skills, employers will hesitate to invest in your compensation.” Technology demands continuous, lifelong learning. 2.4. Distinction of FCJ Build-a-thon Not a 24–48 Hour Hackathon: Short hackathons frequently result in superficial MVP prototypes and pitch decks. A 3- to 6-Month Real-World Building Program: Requires builders to engineer genuine, fully functional architectures on live AWS accounts, mentored by senior architects, and evaluated by external industry judges (enterprise CIOs and IT Directors). 3. Session 2: Career Opportunities at CMC Global & Mentimeter Pulse Survey Host: Ms. Thai Thanh Nhan — Communications & Talent Acquisition Representative, CMC Global. 3.1. About CMC Global The global business division of CMC Corporation, operating across 10+ offices in 30 countries worldwide, with major technical hubs in Hanoi, Da Nang, and Ho Chi Minh City. Introduced the Fresher Tech Camp — a structured talent development initiative in its 4th consecutive year, providing paid internships and full-time promotion pathways. 3.2. Mentimeter AI Demand Survey Attendees participated in an interactive poll regarding their primary daily AI needs:
Top keyword selections included: Coding, Research, Task Automation, Debugging, GenAI, Continuous Learning. This transitioned into the technical discussion: how to architect customized, production-ready AI agents tailored for real enterprise workflows. 4. Session 3: Technical Deep-Dive — Building a Production Triage Bot & Coding Agent on Slack Speaker: Mr. Bui Nhat Truong — Technical Leader at CMC Global (Australia Market), Head of Digital Transformation at Son Kim Group. 4.1. Business Problem & Operational Context CMC Global’s engineering teams are based in Vietnam, while client and business teams operate in Australia across a 3–4 hour timezone difference. When Australian stakeholders report urgent bugs early in their morning, Vietnamese engineers are not yet online. Objective: Construct an autonomous Triage Bot on Slack capable of gathering detailed incident context from stakeholders, cross-referencing monitoring signals (AWS CloudWatch, Datadog, Sumo Logic), and generating structured triage summaries ready for engineers by 8:30 AM. 4.2. “The Full Picture” Architectural Breakdown Mr. Truong delivered a comprehensive walk-through of the Market Slack Bot architecture, powered by the Claude Code / Clawbot Harness Tool:
Core Architectural Components Breakdown: The Soul Layer (SOUL.md — inspired by OpenClaw): Decoupled from core agent logic to define: Persona (friendly, professional), Scope (permitted vs. restricted actions), and Communication Tone. Enables orchestrating distinct specialized sub-agents (Developer, Tester, Reviewer, Jira Updater) within a single request cycle without role collision. Slack Socket Mode: Establishes persistent outbound WebSocket communication, eliminating the need for public IP addresses or inbound firewall openings, significantly reducing attack surfaces. Response Gate (Message Filter & Cost-Aware Routing): Evaluates whether incoming channel messages require action or silence (preventing unwanted banter replies). FinOps Optimization: Routes straightforward queries to lightweight models such as Claude Haiku (~$0.25–$1.00/1M tokens) instead of costlier models like Sonnet/Opus ($3.00–$15.00/1M tokens). Thread-Level Memory Management: Persists conversation context per Slack thread in a database. At each invocation turn, the bot fetches and refines state rather than appending raw unbounded text strings, preventing context window saturation. Resilient Scheduling Engine (“A schedule had to survive a restart”): The bot handles recurring automated tasks, such as reminding engineers about pending Pull Requests across 8 repositories. Because ephemeral containers frequently redeploy and purge OS cron states, schedule configurations are stored in a database and reloaded via an Internal API upon each boot. Guardrails & Protective Hooks: Pre- and post-execution hooks (bash scripts) validate all agent outputs, mitigating hallucinations, data loss, or secret key exposure. Response Gate: Knowing when to stay quiet Scheduler surviving container restarts 4.3. Live Slack Production Demo Mr. Truong demonstrated the bot’s workflow through real-time multi-account testing:
Scenario 1 (Autonomous Follow-up): A stakeholder requests a 1-minute pause → Exactly 60 seconds later, the bot pings to resume information gathering. Scenario 2 (Cloudflare 500 Incident Triage): A user reports a service outage → The bot systematically clarifies error codes, categorizes incident severity, and posts an incident summary to #market-triage. Scenario 3 (Automated Jira Dispatch): A stakeholder provides a CSV file of UUIDs requiring investigation → The bot confirms with an engineer and automatically invokes Jira APIs to generate a fully formatted ticket with the CSV attached. 5. Session 4: Q&A Panel & Hands-on Minigame 5.1. Highlighted Technical Inquiries Question 1: Enterprise Project Context Question: How does the bot acquire enterprise project context and internal policies? Speaker (Mr. Truong): Via Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrated with internal Confluence documentation, ensuring triage decisions align with standard corporate operating procedures automatically. Question 2: Preventing LLM Hallucinations Question: How to prevent AI hallucinations from misrouting emergency channel messages? Speaker (Mr. Truong): Maintain a dual design: deterministic rules (channel mappings, credentials) are strictly hard-coded in configuration files, while natural language reasoning is delegated to the LLM. Question 3: Secure Command Execution Question: How to manage permissions and safety when the bot has rights to execute commands? Speaker (Mr. Truong): Enforce the Principle of Least Privilege, execute agents within isolated sandbox containers, and employ strict hook validators on all inputs and outputs. 5.2. Hands-on Minigame: Structuring SOUL.md Participants drafted specifications for agent behavior. Mr. Truong presented the standard template for enterprise AI agents:
name: TriageBot role: Senior Incident Triage & Support Specialist default_model: claude-3-haiku tone_and_style: internal_engineers: concise, technical, direct, structured external_stakeholders: empathetic, polite, non-technical, clarifying skills: - confluence_search - jira_ticket_creator - log_query_cloudwatch anti_patterns: - Do not expose stack traces or raw database queries to stakeholders. - Never execute destructive commands without human confirmation. out_of_scope: - Financial questions, salary inquiries, contract terms. 6. Personal Takeaways & Practical Applications to EduMedia AI Attending this kick-off provided concrete technical enhancements directly applicable to my EduMedia AI internship project:
Adopting the Soul & Scope Paradigm in Multi-Modal Pipelines: In the EduMedia AI system, I will reinforce role boundaries: the Ingest Lambda (agentsys-ingest) focuses solely on feature extraction; the API Lambda (agentsys-api) handles user routing; and Amazon Bedrock operates with well-scoped system prompts. FinOps Awareness & Model Routing: The Response Gate architecture reinforces my strategy of pairing Amazon Titan Embeddings V2 (256-dimension) with Nova Lite for general catalog search, achieving near-zero idle and inference costs. Cultivating Engineering Resilience: Embracing Mr. Hung’s guidance on hands-on rigor, persistent debugging on live AWS environments, and the long-term value of teamwork. Related Content: 4.1. EduMedia AI — Smart Lecture Storage & Search Engine on AWS Student: Do Tran Minh Phuc · VNU-HCM University of Science (HCMUS)
Internship Period: 17/08/2026 – 01/12/2026 · Amazon Web Services Vietnam LLC (FCAJ Bootcamp)
1. Executive Summary EduMedia AI is an intelligent, multi-modal lecture cataloging and retrieval platform engineered entirely on a Serverless and Generative AI architecture using Amazon Web Services (AWS).
The system addresses the fundamental limitation of traditional camera-roll search by automatically extracting multi-sensory semantics from images, audio, and video files:
Amazon CloudFront & Amazon S3 (Web Hosting): Serves the React Static SPA globally over HTTPS edge delivery backed by agentsys-web-*. Amazon S3 (Private Media Storage): Secure object storage protected by Block All Public Access, SSE-S3 encryption, and short-lived Presigned URLs. Amazon SQS & Dead-Letter Queues (DLQs): Decouples ingestion traffic via agentsys-ingest-queue and three isolated DLQs ensuring resilient zero-data-loss processing. AWS Lambda, Amazon Rekognition & Amazon Transcribe: Orchestrates workers (agentsys-ingest, agentsys-aggregator) invoking Amazon Rekognition (labels, scenes, Vietnamese OCR) and Amazon Transcribe (vi-VN speech-to-text via EventBridge). Amazon Bedrock (Nova Pro / Nova Lite & Titan Embeddings V2): Acts as an AI Query Planner, chunk summarization engine, and 256-d semantic vector engine for hybrid ranking. Amazon DynamoDB: Stores media catalog metadata (AgentSysMediaMetadata) with GSI category-index and DynamoDB Streams for hybrid retrieval and Map-Reduce aggregation. Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon SNS & AWS X-Ray: End-to-end observability with structured JSON logs, distributed X-Ray tracing, and 7 CloudWatch Alarms routing notifications through SNS (agentsys-alerts-topic). 2. Problem Statement In academic and professional environments, students and researchers accumulate thousands of multimodal files: whiteboard notes, lecture slide snapshots, multi-hour voice recordings, and video demos.
Major Inefficiencies in Existing Solutions: Filename-based Search Failure: Mobile uploads default to non-descriptive names (e.g., IMG_20260826_104212.jpg or Voice_001.m4a), providing zero semantic metadata. Costly Commercial DAM Solutions: Enterprise Digital Asset Management (DAM) platforms require 24/7 dedicated servers starting at $50–$200/month, making them impractical for students or small research teams. Weak Vietnamese Natural Language Support: Open-source toolkits struggle with diacritics and domain-specific terminology across Mathematics, Economics, and Philosophy. 3. Goals, Success Criteria & Project Scope ID Objective Pass Condition Responsible AWS Service G1 Ingest API Presigned S3 PUT (TTL 900s); images transition to READY in < 5 seconds (Rekognition), while audio/video initiates asynchronous INDEXING completed via Transcribe + EventBridge. S3, SQS, Lambda, DynamoDB, EventBridge G2 Computer Vision Accurately extracts object labels + Vietnamese OCR text from classroom board snapshots. Amazon Rekognition G3 Speech-to-Text Transcribes Vietnamese speech (vi-VN) from audio/video and synthesizes structured summaries across 5–10 minute segments. Amazon Transcribe, Lambda Aggregator G4 Hybrid Search Natural language queries like “find teacher review for final exam” accurately return relevant media items. Amazon Bedrock, DynamoDB GSI G5 Well-Architected & FinOps 100% Serverless (Scale-to-Zero), $0 idle cost, 7 CloudWatch Alarms + SNS, AWS X-Ray active tracing, and verified Cleanup runbook. CloudWatch, SNS, X-Ray, IAM, SAM CLI Project Scope: In-Scope (PoC Phase): Full asynchronous multimodal ingestion pipeline (images, audio, video), automated AI enrichment (Rekognition, Transcribe vi-VN, Titan Text Embeddings V2 256-d, Nova Pro / Nova Lite), hybrid search over DynamoDB GSI (category-index, capped Candidate Pool of 100 items), CloudFront + S3 React SPA, 143 automated Pytest unit tests, 7 CloudWatch Alarms + X-Ray tracing, and reproducible AWS SAM deployment/teardown. Out-of-Scope (Enterprise Roadmap in Section 5.7): Real-time WebSocket live streaming ASR, multi-tenant Amazon Cognito federation, and dedicated Amazon OpenSearch Serverless / Aurora pgvector clusters for multi-million-record catalogs. 4. Proposed System Architecture End-to-End Data Pipeline Workflow: Frontend Edge & Presigned Upload Flow: Users access the React Web UI SPA distributed globally via Amazon CloudFront CDN backed by Amazon S3 (agentsys-web-*). The client requests a scoped S3 Presigned PUT URL (TTL 900s) from agentsys-api (Lambda) through Amazon API Gateway HTTP API (primary route POST /api/v1/media/upload-url, legacy alias /api/upload-url), then uploads directly to private s3://MediaBucket/uploads/. Asynchronous Ingestion Buffer & 3 DLQs: S3 emits s3:ObjectCreated:* notifications (uploads/ prefix only) into Amazon SQS (agentsys-ingest-queue) configured with ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds = 10 and maxReceiveCount = 3 routing failed records to agentsys-ingest-dlq (14-day retention). Two dedicated DLQs (agentsys-transcribe-dlq and agentsys-aggregator-stream-dlq) safeguard EventBridge and DynamoDB Stream deliveries. Multimodal AI Extraction & Stream Aggregation: agentsys-ingest (Lambda, ScalingConfig: MaximumConcurrency = 5, BatchSize = 5) routes by media type: Images: Calls DetectLabels and DetectText (Vietnamese OCR) concurrently via Amazon Rekognition and generates thumbnails (thumbs/). Audio/Video: Initiates asynchronous Amazon Transcribe (vi-VN) jobs, then processes completion/failure events via Amazon EventBridge (Transcribe Job State Change). Transcripts exceeding 250 KB automatically offload to s3://MediaBucket/transcripts/raw/{file_id}.json (retaining a 15,000-character preview in DynamoDB), while longer lectures are segmented into 5–10 minute silence-aware chunks aggregated asynchronously via DynamoDB Streams and agentsys-aggregator Lambda. Metadata & 256-d Vector Storage: Extracted content is embedded into 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors via Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 (amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0) on Amazon Bedrock and persisted in Amazon DynamoDB (AgentSysMediaMetadata) under On-Demand billing (PAY_PER_REQUEST). Intelligent Hybrid Search & Full-Stack Observability: Upon receiving a query (POST /api/v1/media/agent/query), Amazon Bedrock (us.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 default or amazon.nova-lite-v1:0) parses intent (reusing cached plans via _PLAN_CACHE LRU 256 entries, TTL 3600s), queries GSI category-index with a capped Candidate Pool of 100 items, and ranks results via Cosine Vector Similarity (0.6) + Normalized Keyword Overlap (0.4). All 3 Lambdas emit AWS X-Ray (Tracing: Active) traces, structured CloudWatch Logs (14-day retention), and feed 7 CloudWatch Alarms linked to Amazon SNS (agentsys-alerts-topic). Service Selection Rationale: To achieve optimal performance, high availability, and Zero Idle Cost, AWS services were chosen after rigorous evaluation against architectural alternatives:
Selected AWS Service Evaluated Alternative Cost Optimization Criteria High Availability (HA) Serverless / Managed Model Amazon S3 (Standard Storage) Amazon EFS / Amazon EBS $0.023 / GB / month. 13x cheaper than EFS ($0.30/GB). Direct Presigned URLs offload client upload/download traffic entirely, saving 100% of compute and bandwidth costs on backend APIs. Data durability of 99.999999999% (11 9s) alongside 99.99% designed Availability (99.9% SLA commitment), automatically replicated across at least 3 Availability Zones (AZs) in the Region. Managed Object Storage, eliminating disk volume provisioning, filesystem sizing, and storage server management. Amazon CloudFront (Web SPA CDN) EC2 Reverse Proxy (Nginx) / Public S3 Bucket Includes 1 TB Data Transfer Out & 10M HTTP/HTTPS requests/month Always Free for delivering the React Web SPA (agentsys-web-*), yielding $0.00 idle cost. Global edge points of presence with automatic TLS termination and burst absorption without self-managed proxy fleets. Managed Edge CDN, cleanly separating static Web UI distribution from private media and API endpoints. AWS Lambda (Python 3.12 Runtime) Amazon ECS (Fargate / EC2) $0.00 idle cost (Zero Idle Cost). Metered strictly per millisecond and GB-second during actual event execution. 1M free requests/month under AWS Free Tier. ECS Fargate incurs continuous base charges (~$15 - $30/month/task) even with zero traffic. Default Multi-AZ redundancy across the Region; scales instantaneously from 0 to thousands of concurrent executions without managing Auto Scaling Groups. Pure Serverless FaaS, eliminating OS patching, security kernel upgrades, and container runtime daemon maintenance. Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) Application Load Balancer (ALB) / REST API Low cost of $1.00 / million requests (>70% cheaper than REST API at $3.50/M). Zero idle hourly charges compared to ALB (~$16 - $20/month base LCU cost). Native Multi-AZ fault tolerance; protected against L3/L4 DDoS attacks via default AWS Shield Standard and API Gateway account-level limits paired with application-layer rate limiting. Serverless HTTP API, native CORS handling, direct zero-overhead Lambda proxy routing. API authentication (verify_api_key enforcing X-API-Key / JWT) and rate limiting (slowapi 60 reqs/min/IP) are enforced at the FastAPI application tier. Amazon DynamoDB (On-Demand Mode) Amazon RDS Aurora (PostgreSQL / MySQL) $0.00 idle cost. Metered strictly per actual read/write request units (RRU/WRU) plus 25 GB Always Free storage. Aurora Serverless v2 requires a continuous minimum ACU allocation (~$35 - $60/month). Automatic synchronous data replication across 3 AZs; backed by a 99.99% SLA with single-digit millisecond query latency (<10ms). NoSQL Serverless Database, immune to connection pool exhaustion during Lambda scale bursts; zero schema migration downtime. Amazon SQS & DLQ (Message Queue) Amazon Kinesis Data Streams / Apache Kafka (MSK) $0.40 / million requests. 1 million requests free every month (Always Free). In contrast, Kinesis charges per Shard-hour ($11/month/shard) and MSK requires continuous cluster broker fees ($100+/month). Highly resilient distributed message queue across Multi-AZ (agentsys-ingest-queue 24-hour retention, 3 DLQs 14-day retention), buffering burst loads (MaximumConcurrency = 5) without downstream AI throttling. Fully Managed Queue, automatically batch-triggering Lambda Ingest workers and isolating corrupted payloads into Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ). Amazon Bedrock (Nova Pro / Nova Lite & Titan Embeddings V2) Self-hosted LLM on Amazon EC2 GPU (G4dn / G5) $0.06 / million input tokens (Nova Lite), $0.02 / million input tokens (Titan Embeddings V2), plus Cross-Region Inference (us.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0) costing mere pennies in testing. Self-hosting LLMs on EC2 GPU (g4dn.xlarge or g5.xlarge) costs $380 – $750 USD/month continuously. Foundation models hosted on AWS high-performance GPU clusters with built-in high availability and automated inference load distribution. Serverless GenAI API (FaaS), requiring zero management of GPU hardware, CUDA drivers, vLLM containers, or inference scaling clusters. Amazon Rekognition & Transcribe Custom self-trained ML models on EC2 Amazon Transcribe billed at official rate $0.024 / minute ($0.0004 / second). Rekognition billed at $0.001 / API call (DetectLabels + DetectText = $0.002 / image). Eliminates R&D, data labeling, model training, and continuous hosting overhead. Purpose-built AWS AI services backed by 99.9% SLAs and automatic elastic concurrency. Pre-trained Managed AI Services: Transcribe natively optimized for Vietnamese speech-to-text (vi-VN); Rekognition handles object labeling (DetectLabels) and slide text/title extraction (DetectText) out-of-the-box without custom ML training. 5. AWS Well-Architected Framework Evaluation (6 Pillars) The architecture is comprehensively evaluated against the 6 pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework and the Serverless Lens:
Audit Parameter Verification Details on AWS Assessment Tool AWS Well-Architected Tool Workload Name EduMedia AI Workload ID 13f51f4fbcb8f084f550fe07020d295e (Region: us-east-1) Review Owner Do Tran Minh Phuc (Student ID: 23120156 · Account: 181040156515) Applied Lenses AWS Well-Architected Framework & Serverless Lens High-Risk Issues (HRIs) 0 High Risks (100% Best Practice Compliance) 1. Security IAM Least-Privilege: Execution roles are strictly decoupled across all 3 Lambda functions (agentsys-ingest scoped to S3 uploads/ & Rekognition/Transcribe; agentsys-aggregator scoped to DynamoDB Streams & Bedrock refinement; agentsys-api scoped to DynamoDB GSI & Bedrock query planning). Storage Protection: S3 enforces Block All Public Access, SSE-S3 (AES-256) server-side encryption, and scoped short-lived Presigned URLs (PUT: 900s / 15 min, GET: 3600s / 60 min). Secret Management: Zero hardcoded credentials; API authentication uses X-API-Key secured via CloudFormation NoEcho alongside JWT Bearer token validation. 2. Reliability Traffic Decoupling: SQS (agentsys-ingest-queue) buffers burst ingestion traffic (MaximumConcurrency = 5), preventing Lambda concurrency exhaustion. Failure Isolation: Failed payloads are routed after 3 retries into three dedicated DLQs (agentsys-ingest-dlq, agentsys-transcribe-dlq, agentsys-aggregator-stream-dlq), triggering immediate CloudWatch Alarms via SNS. DynamoDB 400KB Item Guard (S3-Offloading): Transcripts exceeding 250KB are automatically offloaded to Amazon S3 (transcripts/raw/{file_id}.json), storing a 15,000-character preview and S3 URI in DynamoDB to safely maintain items well below the 400KB limit while preserving instant UI access. 3. Performance Efficiency Vector Compression (Titan V2 Native 256-d): Configures dimensions = 256 with L2 normalization natively on Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2—achieving a 75% storage reduction compared to Titan V2’s default 1024 dimensions (and 83% reduction vs Titan V1’s 1536 dimensions) while preserving semantic recall. DynamoDB GSI Partitioning (category-index): GSI partition routing paired with a bounded 100-item Candidate Pool eliminates full-table scans, reducing RCU cost and latency by over 90% (<40ms). Lambda Warm-Container Reuse: Boto3 client connections and TLS handshakes persist across warm Lambda invocations, avoiding 50–120ms reconnection overhead on every SQS message or API request. In-Memory Query Plan Cache (_PLAN_CACHE): LRU caching (max 256 entries, 1h TTL) of parsed search plans speeds up repeated query responses by 3.7x and saves 100% of LLM token costs. 4. Cost Optimization (FinOps) Scale-to-Zero Model: Idle infrastructure costs exactly $0.00 USD. Bedrock LRU Caching: In-memory query caching eliminates token costs for recurring search queries. S3 Lifecycle Rules: Automatic expiration for temporary files in transcripts/ after 7 days (ExpirationInDays: 7). 5. Operational Excellence Infrastructure as Code (IaC): The entire stack is provisioned via AWS SAM (agent_sys/infra/template.yaml), enabling single-command teardown via scripts/cleanup.sh and sam delete. Observability & Tracing: All 3 Lambdas enable AWS X-Ray (Tracing: Active), emit structured JSON CloudWatch Logs (14-day retention), publish custom metrics (MediaIngested, MediaIngestFailed), and enforce 7 CloudWatch Alarms (agentsys-api-errors, agentsys-ingest-errors, agentsys-aggregator-errors, agentsys-ingest-failed, agentsys-ingest-dlq, agentsys-aggregator-stream-dlq, agentsys-transcribe-dlq) linked to SNS Topic agentsys-alerts-topic. 6. High Two-Stage Hybrid Search Architecture: Route queries through DynamoDB GSI (category-index) into a capped Candidate Pool (CANDIDATE_POOL_LIMIT = 100 newest items) inside Lambda RAM for hybrid Cosine (0.6) + Keyword (0.4) scoring, paired with compact 256-d Titan V2 vectors and an in-memory LRU _PLAN_CACHE (256 entries, 1h TTL) saving 100% of repeat query tokens. High Strict S3 prefix segregation (uploads/ trigger only, writing artifacts to thumbs/ and transcripts/); configure three Dead-Letter Queues (agentsys-ingest-dlq, agentsys-transcribe-dlq, agentsys-aggregator-stream-dlq) with maxReceiveCount = 3 to isolate failing messages. 4 Rekognition Video Cost Trap ($0.10/min) & Long Lecture Processing: Rekognition Video is extremely costly ($0.10/min/feature = $50 for 250 mins), while long voice recordings risk lengthy synchronous processing. High Intelligent Multi-Modal Tiering: Route video/audio files asynchronously to Amazon Transcribe (vi-VN, $0.024/min); split transcripts via silence-aware pipeline/chunking.py into 5–10 minute logical segments refined by agentsys-aggregator over DynamoDB Streams and embedded with Titan Text Embeddings V2 (supporting up to 8,192 tokens, emitting compact 256-d vectors); reserve Rekognition Image ($0.001/API call, or $0.002/image for DetectLabels + DetectText) for static slides/boards (>95% cost savings). 5 Lambda Synchronous Wait on Batch Transcription: Batch transcription takes 1–3 minutes. Polling synchronously with sleep() inside Lambda inflates GB-sec runtime by 100x. High 100% Asynchronous Event-Driven Design: agentsys-ingest invokes StartTranscriptionJob() and exits immediately. Amazon EventBridge captures `Transcribe Job State Change (COMPLETED 6 S3 Egress Costs & Private Media Access Control: Directly hosting Web SPA bundles from uncached buckets or exposing raw media risks S3 egress fees ($0.09/GB past 100GB) and security leaks. Medium Separate Web UI and private media storage cleanly: serve the React Static Web SPA (agentsys-web-*) via Amazon CloudFront CDN (leveraging CloudFront’s Always Free 1 TB Data Transfer Out & 10M requests/month), while keeping MediaBucket blocked from public access (Block All Public Access = true) behind scoped S3 Presigned URLs (PUT: 900s / GET: 3600s). 7 DynamoDB 400KB Item Limit & Logs/Polling Overhead: Lengthy transcripts exceeding DynamoDB 400KB single-item limits; unbounded logs or aggressive SQS polling inflating baseline bills. Medium Automatic S3-offloading for transcript payloads exceeding 250 KB (s3://MediaBucket/transcripts/raw/{file_id}.json), storing a 15,000-character preview and URI in DynamoDB. Blog 1 - Serverless Media Processing: Why I Avoid Direct S3 Lambda Triggers Publication Status: Approved & Published — View Facebook Post
Deconstructs the three critical failure modes of push-based S3 direct Lambda triggers: internal unmonitored queues, concurrency exhaustion cascading downstream, and silent event drops. Details the pull-based SQS + DLQ Claim Check architecture with ScalingConfig: MaximumConcurrency = 5 and ReportBatchItemFailures. Blog 2 - DynamoDB Query Optimization: Limitations of FilterExpression and the Global Secondary Index Solution Publication Status: Submitted on AWS Study Group VN (Pending Admin Approval — screenshot proof attached inside page)

title: Blog 3 - Optimizing Docker Build Time on AWS CodeBuild with Amazon ECR Remote Cache
content:
Author: Nguyen Thanh Phuc Program: First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) 2026 — AWS Vietnam Topic Domain: AWS CI/CD & Cost Optimization — Docker Layer Caching on AWS CodeBuild & Amazon ECR Publication Channel: AWS Study Group Community (Facebook) (Submitted — Pending Admin Approval) Optimizing Docker Build Time on AWS CodeBuild with Amazon ECR Remote Cache In modern CI/CD workflows, packaging applications with Docker is a standard step. However, AWS CodeBuild provisions completely ephemeral, isolated build environments for each execution. Repeatedly downloading base images and rebuilding every layer from scratch wastes compute minutes and slows down deployment pipelines.
Transitioning from AWS CodeBuild’s default local cache mechanism to a Remote Cache architecture backed by Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) provides persistent layer reuse across spaced-out builds and cuts infrastructure overhead.
1. Limitations of Default CodeBuild Local Cache Many CI/CD pipelines initially rely solely on CodeBuild’s built-in LOCAL_DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE option. In production usage, this mechanism exhibits two fundamental drawbacks:
Ephemeral, Best-Effort Storage:
CodeBuild local storage is provisioned on temporary host instances. Local layer caching is only effective when consecutive builds run closely back-to-back on the same cached fleet. Lack of Persistence Across Time Gaps:
When builds occur hours or days apart, the underlying local cache volume is reclaimed. Even with LOCAL_DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE enabled, CodeBuild encounters cache misses and must re-download base images and reinstall every dependency layer from Layer 1, driving up build duration and billable compute minutes. 2. Architecture: Multi-Layer Caching with Amazon ECR Remote Cache To achieve durable cross-build layer caching, the cache backend must live outside the ephemeral CodeBuild container. The workflow uses Docker Buildx backed by a containerd image store and Amazon ECR:
CodeBuild (Install phase) ──> Enable containerd via docker buildx ──> CodeBuild (Build phase) ──> Pull/Push Cache (--cache-from / --cache-to) <──> Amazon ECR Figure: Architectural comparison between ephemeral Local Cache and durable Multi-Layer + Amazon ECR Remote Cache on AWS CodeBuild.
Core Components: Amazon ECR: Acts as a long-term persistent remote backend storing cached Docker layer manifests alongside final application images. AWS CodeBuild: Configured in buildspec.yml to proactively pull cached layers prior to building and export updated cache layers upon completion. Containerd Image Store (docker buildx): The legacy default Docker driver does not support exporting build cache directly to a remote registry. An isolated builder instance backed by containerd must be initialized during the install phase. 3. Build Mechanics & Reference Configuration 3.1. Enforcing Remote Cache Pull and Push (--cache-from / --cache-to) During the build phase, passing --cache-from instructs Buildx to query the ECR cache manifest before rebuilding layers, while --cache-to (with image-manifest=true) packages and pushes updated layer metadata back to ECR.
version: 0.2 phases: install: commands: # Initialize buildx builder supporting registry cache export - docker buildx create --name ecr-builder --driver docker-container --use pre_build: commands: - aws ecr get-login-password --region $AWS_DEFAULT_REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $AWS_ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION.amazonaws.com build: commands: - | docker buildx build \ --cache-from type=registry,ref=$ECR_REPO:buildcache \ --cache-to type=registry,ref=$ECR_REPO:buildcache,mode=max,image-manifest=true \ -t $ECR_REPO:latest \ --push . 3.2. Incremental Change Handling & Performance Impact Cold Run (Initial Cache Miss): On the first run before cache manifests exist, the pipeline builds all layers end-to-end (~10 minutes) and uploads both the application image and the buildcache manifest to Amazon ECR. Subsequent Runs (Code or Dockerfile Changes): Whenever source code or downstream Dockerfile instructions change, Docker automatically reuses every unchanged upstream layer from ECR and only rebuilds invalidated stages, bringing observed build time down to ~6 minutes (and delivering up to a 25% build time reduction in complex multi-stage builds). 3.3. Multi-Layer Cache Strategy (Local + Remote Fallback) Adopting ECR Remote Cache does not require disabling CodeBuild’s LOCAL_DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE. Keeping both enabled establishes a resilient two-tier cache hierarchy:
Tier 1 (Warm Container): CodeBuild serves unchanged layers instantaneously from local disk cache whenever a warm host instance is available. Tier 2 (Persistent Fallback): Whenever the local host cache has expired or rotated out, CodeBuild falls back seamlessly to Amazon ECR remote cache layers instead of rebuilding from scratch. 4. Practical Comparison: Local Cache Only vs. Multi-Layer ECR Remote Cache Evaluation Criteria Default LOCAL_DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE docker buildx (containerd) + ECR Remote Cache Cache Persistence Ephemeral (evicted after hours/days) Persistent in Amazon ECR repository Registry Cache Export Local host only Supported via containerd + image-manifest=true Observed Build Time ~10 minutes on spaced-out cold runs ~6 minutes incremental (up to 25% faster multi-stage) Compute Cost Control Repeated cold rebuilds waste build minutes Predictable savings across spaced CI/CD triggers 5. Key Takeaways CI/CD Optimization Goes Beyond Build Success: Controlling per-run compute duration directly reduces pipeline wait times and AWS CodeBuild billing. Containerd Driver Is Mandatory: Default Docker drivers cannot export registry cache; configuring docker buildx in the install phase unlocks remote layer manifests cleanly. Combine Tiers for Speed & Durability: Pairing LOCAL_DOCKER_LAYER_CACHE for rapid back-to-back commits with Amazon ECR Remote Cache as persistent backup delivers smooth continuous integration at minimal operational complexity. #AWS #CodeBuild #AmazonECR #Docker #DevOps #CI_CD #CostOptimization #FCAJ Publication Evidence (Pending Admin Approval):
